study_identification_part.si4_title: Individualized cortical thickness asymmetry in Autism Spectrum Disorders and Schizophrenia

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To investigate whether deviations from normative cortical thickness asymmetry are disproportionately represented among individuals with ASD or SZ by applying normative modeling to a large, multi-scanner sample.

As per previous work, we excluded 682 images with an IQR >2.8... Finally, as per previous work, images were removed if the maximum, absolute, within-dataset centered Euler number was larger than 10... This was the case for five images.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: Scanner was included as a covariate in the Bayesian Linear Regression normative model. Post-hoc validation was performed using one-versus-all linear support vector machines to classify scan sites from z-scores, with resulting balanced accuracy near chance level (50%) indicating minimal residual site effects.

A mean balanced accuracy near chance level (50%) served as an indicator that the observed deviations were minimally influenced by residual site effects, which was confirmed for our main approach...

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group differences in the proportion of individuals with extreme z-scores were tested using permuted chi-square tests with FDR correction. Group differences in whole-brain AI z-scores were assessed with Welch's t-tests. Group differences in the number of deviant regions per individual were tested with the Mann-Whitney U test. A multivariate analysis using t-SNE and k-medoid clustering was used to test for an association between the inter-regional pattern of deviance and diagnosis.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Individualized deviations in whole brain, regional, and inter-regional cortical thickness asymmetry in individuals with ASD and SZ are largely accounted for by normative variation, questioning the utility of this metric as a biomarker for these disorders.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study found no significant differences in whole brain or regional cortical thickness asymmetry deviations between individuals with ASD and healthy controls. For SZ, a higher proportion of individuals showed supra-normal asymmetry in only one of 160 regions (superior temporal cortex), with a small effect size (ω = 0.14). The SZ group had a statistically higher average number of deviant regions per individual, but a multivariate analysis of the spatial pattern of deviations found no relationship with diagnosis for either ASD or SZ. The authors conclude that individual abnormal asymmetry is generally not a feature of these disorders.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: 1. The training dataset could benefit from greater geographic diversity. 2. Multi-center data lacks deep phenotyping (e.g., incomplete data on handedness, IQ, symptoms). 3. Clinical sample sizes might be insufficient to detect small, distinct patient subgroups. 4. The analysis was restricted to cortical thickness, and other metrics like cortical volume or shape might yield different findings.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: This study has limitations. While the present multi-center study benefited from a substantial training set... larger and more heterogeneous datasets, incorporating data from all continents may be important... While multi-center studies are necessary to increase sample size it also results in including datasets lacking deep phenotyping. Hence, information about handedness, IQ and symptomatology was incomplete. ...larger (multicenter) clinical samples may enable the identification of distinct clusters of patients exhibiting significant deviance... Finally, we focused on cortical thickness which is a property of cortical size. Other size properties such as cortical volume or novel approaches focusing on cortical shape... may lead to improved clustering...

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study's main findings were validated through multiple replication analyses to ensure their robustness. These included: 1) using a higher-resolution brain parcellation (1000 regions), 2) using an alternative image processing pipeline for calculating asymmetry ('xhemi'), and 3) restricting the analysis to male participants only. The results were consistent across all these approaches. The study also explicitly tested for confounding effects of handedness and IQ and found none.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: The study utilized a 'within-site-split' methodology for creating the training and test sets, meaning that data from the same 20 scanners were present in both sets, though the individuals were different. This controls for scanner effects but means the model was not tested on a completely external, different-domain dataset.
